derivation:
This is the plan's own track, not an observed one. Every position is a point the operation order names — the departure from Hitokappu Bay, the standby point, the approaching point, and the two launch positions given as distances due north of point Z — and every time is the hour the order gives, converted from Tokyo time (UTC+9) to UTC. The order's hours and the American accounts of the same morning agree to the minute once Hawaii's standard time of the day, ten and a half hours behind Greenwich, is used: the order's 0130 on X Day is 0600 in Honolulu, which is when the American histories say the first wave took off.

Two waypoints are marked low and the reasons are different. The standby point is low because the document contradicts itself about it: p. 7 gives 42°N 165°W and p. 21 gives 42°N 170°W, and the pack takes the second without claiming to know which is right. The last waypoint is low because it is not a position at all but a heading: the order says the force was to withdraw northward at about 24 knots and return by way of an assembly point at 30°N 165°E, and nothing this project could open records where the force actually was after the aircraft came back aboard. Between the named points the line is a straight line and the force did not sail one.
notes:
The two legs of 6–7 December run above this pack's declared sustained speed for the striking force and inside its limit, so the pace check reports them as warnings. That is correct and it is left standing: the order itself distinguishes the 12–14 knots of the passage from the roughly 24 knots of the run-in, and these are the run-in.

Re-examined under sand-23b.61 and left unchanged. Two things the waypoints do that a wrong date or a wrong position would not: the leg between the two launch positions is 24.0 knots of straight-line displacement, which is the order's own figure for the run-in, and the two positions are 230.1 and 200.1 nautical miles due north of the latitude of Pearl Harbor, which is where the order puts them. The leg before them is 22.2 knots of displacement across a track the force did not sail straight, so its speed through the water was higher still and the ordered 24 knots covers it.

sources.note: departure from Hitokappu Bay on 26 November at 12–14 knots (pp. 7, 21); the standby point (pp. 7, 21, giving two different longitudes); the approaching point at 32°N 157°W (p. 10); the turn south at 0700 X-1 Day at about 24 knots and the two launch positions and hours (p. 13); the assembly point at 30°N 165°E for the return (p. 11)

ch. 5 — the American account of the same moment: the striking force “reached its launching position 200 miles north of Oahu exactly on schedule, at 0600 on the morning of 7 December (0100 on the 8th, Tokyo time)”. Its Tokyo time is half an hour off the operation order's own, which is the arithmetic of Hawaii's 1941 offset; the pack follows the order

derivation: **Hypothetical, and drawn as such.** Not a track anybody recorded: the force holds south of its recovery position through the afternoon of 7 December instead of turning away, closes to about the second wave's launching distance to fly a third strike, and recovers it towards dusk. The speeds are inside the ones the operation order gives for this force; nothing else about it is documented, because it did not happen.

sources.note: the launching distances and the speeds this branch reuses; the order itself contains no third wave

derivation: Three positions and no more. The launch point is 230 nautical miles due north of point Z, as the operation order gives it, taken from the latitude of Pearl Harbor; the launch hour is the order's 0130 on X Day in Tokyo time, which is 0600 in Honolulu. The middle waypoint is the harbour at 0755 Honolulu time, when the American air force history records the first aircraft observed over Oahu. The last is the return towards the carriers at 1000, by which time the American accounts say the raid was over and the aircraft were heading north; it is marked low because the recovery position is interpolated along the striking force's own track and is not documented. The formation did not fly a straight line — it came down the west side of the island — and the pack does not pretend otherwise.

sources.note: ch. 6 — “Exactly on schedule, at 0600 on the 7th, orders for the take-off were given” and “At 0755 single-engine planes were observed southeast of the Hickam Field hangar line heading for Pearl Harbor.” No pages: see the pack README
ch. VI — “By 1000 the raid was over and the Japanese planes were heading north toward the carriers.”

derivation: The same construction as the first wave: the launch point is the order's 200 nautical miles due north of point Z and the hour is its 0245 on X Day, Tokyo time, which is 0715 in Honolulu; the middle waypoint is the harbour at 0840, when the American air force history records the second attack beginning. The two sources disagree about the launch by half an hour — the air force history has the second wave taking off forty-five minutes behind the first, the order has it seventy-five minutes behind — and the pack follows the order, because the order's interval is the one that agrees with the striking force closing from 230 to 200 nautical miles at the speed the same order sets. The last waypoint is the recovery on the carriers' track and is marked low.

sources.note: the launch position and hour, and the interval between the waves
ch. 6 — “At 0840 horizontal and dive bombers renewed the attack”, and the second wave taking off “forty-five minutes later”, which is the disagreement noted in the derivation
